turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Dr. Smith. Yes, well, it’s... it’s a bit of a long story, I suppose, but I’ll try to explain exactly what’s been happening. I’ve been spending most of my time at home lately—I have this lovely little apartment, an older building, you know, the kind with the very thick plaster walls where you really shouldn't be able to hear your neighbors at all. But recently, I keep hearing these voices. And they aren't muffled or distant, they are incredibly clear. 

It’s women, specifically, whispering right from behind the walls. At first, I thought it was just the building settling or some sort of strange acoustic trick with the ventilation, but then it started happening when I go out, too. I like to visit the art museum on weekday mornings when it's quiet, and I’ll be standing there in a completely empty room, not a guard or another visitor in sight, and the whispering starts up again from behind the gallery walls. 

They’re always talking about the archive. These women keep telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive, sorting them out, insisting on what goes where and which ones are important. It’s just so vivid, and it happens so often now, whether I'm sitting on my own sofa or standing completely alone in a museum room... I just don't understand how the voices follow me, or how they know so much about the photographs, but it's been very overwhelming to listen to them all day.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly describes hearing clear voices of women whispering from behind walls when no one is there, which is a clear auditory hallucination.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from hearing these voices, have you been experiencing any periods where your mood feels unusually low, or conversely, periods where you feel extremely energetic or elated?
turns.patient_response:
Well, energetic... energetic is almost too small a word for it, really. I mean, yes, I do have these days, and they are quite extraordinary. I’ll wake up and I just feel absolutely radiant. It’s as if there’s a literal light glowing right inside my chest, and I feel so completely... chosen. Like I have this profound, undeniable purpose that I am meant to fulfill, and everything in the world suddenly makes perfect sense. I have a plan, you see, a very important plan that requires my full attention, and on those days, I have all the energy in the universe to see it through. I can just go and go and go, organizing and moving, and it feels glorious. 

But... well, the difficulty comes when I have to interact with other people who just don't understand the magnitude of it all. If someone—anyone, really, a neighbor in the hall, or a clerk at the store, or someone on the telephone—if they question my plan, or if they look at me and tell me I need to just slow down and take a breath... oh, Dr. Smith, I become furious. Just absolutely furious. It’s a sudden, white-hot anger that takes over my whole body. Because it doesn't feel like they're just being helpful or giving me advice. It feels exactly as if they are trying to erase me. Like by telling me to stop, they want to wipe out my purpose and just erase my entire existence right then and there. So, yes, I suppose you could say I get extremely energetic and elated, but it becomes very intense and very upsetting when people try to stand in my way and diminish what I'm meant to be doing.

symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient describes periods of feeling 'absolutely radiant' and elated, which can quickly turn into 'white-hot anger' and fury when thwarted.

symptom_reasoning.S035: The patient exhibits grandiosity, stating they feel 'chosen' and have a 'profound, undeniable purpose.'
symptom_reasoning.S040: The patient describes an intense drive to execute a 'very important plan,' spending their energy 'organizing and moving' to see it through.

turns.doctor_question: Are there periods, perhaps lasting for two weeks or more, where you hear these voices even when you are not feeling that intense, radiant energy or the extreme anger?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, actually. Yes, there definitely was a time like that. It was... oh, let me think, it must have been earlier this year, right around the time the weather started to turn and the days were getting a bit longer, but it was still quite chilly in the mornings. I remember it vividly because I wasn't feeling that... that radiant glow at all. I wasn't bursting with energy or feeling like I had to rush around fulfilling my plan. In fact, my mood was quite steady, just sort of... ordinary, I suppose. I was just going about my days, making my tea, reading by the window, not feeling grand or particularly angry with anyone. 

But the voices—the whispers—they didn't stop. Not at all. For several weeks, it must have been at least three or four weeks, I would still hear those women whispering from behind the plaster in my apartment. They were still sorting the photographs, still murmuring about the archive, even though I didn't feel that intense drive myself. And it wasn't just the walls, Dr. Smith. During that same period, when I was feeling perfectly calm and not at all elevated, I was absolutely certain—and I still am, really—that the people from the arts council, the ones connected to the museum, were monitoring my telephone. Every time I picked up the receiver, I could hear this faint clicking, this hollow sort of echo, and I just knew they were listening in to see if I was talking about the archive. So, yes, the voices and the monitoring, they were very much present for weeks, completely separate from those days when I feel so full of light and purpose.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, certain belief that people from the arts council were monitoring her telephone.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient reports hearing women whispering from behind the plaster in her apartment for several weeks.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever experienced a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt deeply sad, hopeless, or lost interest in almost all of your usual activities?
turns.patient_response:
Well, deeply sad... hopeless... it’s not quite like that. It’s not that I’m sitting around crying or feeling this heavy despair, Dr. Smith. It’s more of a... a profound emptiness, I suppose you could call it. A sort of blankness that just settles over everything. 

There are these long stretches, sometimes weeks at a time, where I just... stop. I have this lovely little kitchen, with a window that gets the morning light perfectly, and I used to keep these little terracotta pots of herbs on the windowsill—basil, rosemary, a bit of thyme. But during these stretches, I’ll just sit at the kitchen table for hours. I’ll just sit there, staring at the pots, and I watch the soil dry out until it pulls away from the sides of the clay, and the leaves turn brown and crumble, and I just... I don't water them. I know they need water, I know the pitcher is right there by the sink, but I just can't bring myself to care enough to stand up and do it. 

And it’s not just the plants. I have friends, lovely people I’ve known for years, who will call and leave messages. They’ll invite me out—"Oh, let's go to that new gallery opening downtown," or, "There's a wonderful chamber music concert this Friday, I have an extra ticket." And usually, I would love that. The arts have always been such a vital part of my life. But when this blankness hits, I just let the machine take the calls. I listen to their voices echoing in the living room, and I don't pick up. I don't call them back. I don't feel even a flicker of interest in the gallery, or the music, or seeing anyone at all. It’s just... nothing. A great, vast nothingness where my enthusiasm used to be. It's so strange, because it's the complete opposite of that radiant energy I was telling you about, but it's just as real, and it just goes on and on until I feel like I've turned to dust right along with my poor herbs.

symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient describes avolition (unable to bring herself to water plants), asociality (ignoring calls from friends), and anhedonia.
symptom_reasoning.S024: Although the patient denies sadness or crying, she explicitly describes experiencing a 'profound emptiness' and 'blankness' that settles over everything.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports a complete loss of enthusiasm and not feeling 'even a flicker of interest' in activities she usually loves, like concerts and gallery openings.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient explicitly denies feeling hopeless or experiencing 'heavy despair'.

turns.doctor_question: During those weeks when you feel that profound emptiness and lose interest in everything, do you also notice significant changes in your sleep patterns, such as sleeping much more or much less than usual?
turns.patient_response:
Sleep... well, sleep is a peculiar thing during those times, Dr. Smith. It’s not that I’m tossing and turning, or that I’m sleeping the days away entirely, although the days certainly do blur together when you’re just sitting at the kitchen table watching the dust motes drift through the air. I mean, I suppose I haven't really kept a strict log of my hours or anything like that. When the blankness is there, time just sort of... stretches out, like a rubber band that's been pulled too far and loses its snap. 

I don't recall suddenly sleeping for fourteen hours a day, or lying awake staring at the ceiling all night, if that's what you mean. The routine of it just sort of fades into the background, much like the ringing of the telephone or the dry soil in the pots. I go to bed when it's dark, eventually, and I get up when it's light, eventually, but the quality of it, the exact hours... I haven't really noticed a dramatic shift in the actual sleeping part of it. It's more about what I'm *not* doing when I am awake, you see. The waking hours are so empty that they almost feel like a different kind of sleep, a waking slumber where my body is upright but my spirit is just... dormant. So, no, I wouldn't say my sleep itself changes all that much, not in any significant way that stands out from the general fog of it all.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes their waking hours as 'so empty' and their spirit as 'dormant,' confirming a state of profound emptiness.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient describes sitting and watching dust motes, ignoring the ringing telephone and dry plants, and emphasizes what they are 'not doing,' indicating a severe loss of interest and motivation.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient explicitly denies significant changes in their sleep patterns, stating they do not sleep excessively or lie awake all night.

turns.doctor_question: During those times when you feel that profound emptiness, have you ever felt so slowed down physically and mentally that you were unable to get out of bed or perform basic daily tasks for most of the day?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, unable to get out of bed? No, no, it’s never been quite like that. Even when that heavy, gray blankness is pressing down on the entire apartment, I still go through the physical motions. I always get up. 

I’ll push the duvet back—it’s this lovely, heavy down comforter I bought years ago at a little boutique that used to be over on 4th Street, though I think it’s just another coffee shop now—and I swing my legs over the side of the mattress. I always put my slippers on right away because the hardwood floors get so terribly cold, especially since the building is older and the drafts just seem to seep right up through the floorboards. And then I walk down the hallway to the bathroom. I wash my face, I brush my teeth... I mean, I’m not moving at a brisk pace, certainly. I’m not marching around with that brilliant, radiant energy I told you about earlier, but I’m not physically stuck in the bed, if that makes sense. 

I make my way to the kitchen every single morning. I fill the kettle, I turn on the stove. It’s just... well, once the tea is made, and I sit down at that little oak table by the window with those poor dying herbs I mentioned, that’s when the stopping happens. The physical ability to walk and dress myself and pour the hot water, that’s all perfectly intact. My limbs work just fine. My mind knows how to tie my robe and find my favorite mug in the cupboard. It’s the *purpose* that’s missing, Dr. Smith, not the physical machinery of my body. 

I can walk around the apartment all day if I choose to, shuffling from the living room to the kitchen and back again, maybe tracing the floral patterns in the Persian rug with the toe of my slipper. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm paralyzed or unable to perform my basic grooming or get out from under the covers. It's just that once those very basic, automatic morning things are finished, there is absolutely nothing left inside to drive me to do anything else, so I just sit. But the getting up part, the basic tasks of starting the day... no, I've never lost the ability to do those.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes a 'heavy, gray blankness' pressing down on them, confirming a persistent state of emptiness.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient states that their 'purpose is missing' and there is 'absolutely nothing left inside to drive me to do anything else,' indicating a profound loss of motivation.
symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient explicitly denies being physically slowed down to the point of being unable to get out of bed or perform basic daily tasks, stating their physical ability is 'perfectly intact.'

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over the past year, have there been any periods of at least two weeks where you experienced these voices and the feeling that you were being monitored while you were in a state of 'radiant energy' or 'extreme anger'?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yes. Yes, they absolutely overlap, Dr. Smith. In fact, just this past year, there was this extraordinarily intense stretch... oh, it must have been a good three weeks or more. You see, I had thrown myself into this massive undertaking with some historical archives. I was sleeping... heavens, maybe two or three hours a night at most? But I didn't even feel tired! I had that exact radiant energy we talked about, just coursing through my veins like electricity. I was racing from one archive task to another, sorting through these towering stacks of documents, cross-referencing files, making these brilliant, rapid-fire connections that I just knew no one else had ever noticed before. 

And right in the middle of all that frantic pacing and sorting, while I was practically vibrating with purpose... that's when the women's voices were the most persistent. They were right there with me, whispering and murmuring while I worked. And I knew—I was absolutely, undeniably certain—that the museum board was tracking my work. I could feel their presence, you know? I knew they were monitoring every single paper I filed, every note I made. I'd be sitting there at three in the morning, the only light coming from my desk lamp—it has this beautiful antique green glass shade that casts such a peculiar, theatrical glow across the papers—and my mind would be racing a mile a minute with the archives, and all the while, those women would be speaking to me. I could just feel the heavy gaze of the museum board bearing down on me, watching my every move to see what I would uncover next. So, yes, the boundless energy and the voices and the monitoring... they were all happening all at once, just tangled up together for weeks on end.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over your entire life, could you tell me if you have experienced these voices or the feeling of being monitored for a total of at least six months, even if there were times when the symptoms were less intense?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, six months... well, let me think about that. No, it’s been longer than that, Dr. Smith. I can tell you quite specifically, it’s been about eight months now. 

I know this for a fact because... well, you see, eight months ago I had just begun a very particular, very delicate phase of my archiving project. I was organizing this fascinating series of correspondence—mostly letters written on this incredibly thin, fragile onion-skin paper that you have to handle with the absolute utmost delicacy, or it just crumbles right under your fingertips like dried leaves. I had set up a special workstation on the dining table to get the best natural light, though of course, I had to keep the blinds drawn halfway to protect the century-old ink from fading in the sun. 

And that is exactly when it started. That’s when the women's voices first began murmuring while I was reading. They were just whispering just over my shoulder, commenting on the letters. And that was the exact same time that this absolute certainty settled over me—this undeniable knowledge—that people were watching my archive. 

So, yes, it has been eight months. And it hasn’t stopped since, not for a single day. Sometimes, I suppose, it’s a bit quieter. Perhaps the women are just whispering out in the hallway instead of right in my ear, or the feeling of those eyes on me is just a slight prickle on the back of my neck instead of a heavy, suffocating weight... but they are always there. Every single day for eight months I have lived with them watching my work, scrutinizing my files, whispering about what I’m doing with the papers. It’s quite exhausting, really, having an invisible audience for eight months straight, especially when you are trying to concentrate on such delicate historical materials. You'd think they would get bored of watching me sort papers after eight months, but no, the certainty that they are watching is just as strong today as it was when I first opened those onion-skin letters.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes an absolute certainty and undeniable knowledge that people are watching their archive and scrutinizing their files.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient reports hearing women's voices murmuring and whispering over their shoulder every day for the past eight months.
